Basics of Data Visualization Using ggplot2

Keiko Bridwell

This tutorial is intended to introduce you to the basic fundamentals of the ggplot2 data visualization package in R. It demonstrates how to build, layer by layer, three of the most common types of graphs that you will encounter: scatterplots, bar graphs, and line graphs. Features covered include: basic ggplot syntax, geoms (geometric objects), labels and titles, preset themes, and basic customization.

Setting up your R session

  • Today’s tutorial focuses on using the ggplot2 package for data visualization. We will also use the dplyr package to reshape our data.
  • Load ggplot2 and dplyr to this R session, as below. If you haven’t used these packages before, you need to install them first.
# install.packages("ggplot2")
# install.packages("dplyr")
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
  • We will be using the penguins dataset from the pre-loaded package datasets.
  • Inspect the penguins dataset and look at its documentation.
head(penguins)
##   species    island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass    sex year
## 1  Adelie Torgersen     39.1     18.7         181      3750   male 2007
## 2  Adelie Torgersen     39.5     17.4         186      3800 female 2007
## 3  Adelie Torgersen     40.3     18.0         195      3250 female 2007
## 4  Adelie Torgersen       NA       NA          NA        NA   <NA> 2007
## 5  Adelie Torgersen     36.7     19.3         193      3450 female 2007
## 6  Adelie Torgersen     39.3     20.6         190      3650   male 2007
  • You can look at the dataset’s documentation, which describes the variables and tells what units they are in, by typing ?penguins into the console.

Structure of ggplot code

  • In ggplot2, a graph is built in layers:
    • ggplot(): specifies the data and variables
    • geoms: add a type of shape (points, lines, bars) to the plot
    • labels: add titles and axis labels
    • theme: customization
  • In the next section, we will demonstrate how to build a basic scatterplot from start to finish using geom_point. We will then create bar charts with geom_bar and line graphs with geom_line and explore how to add additional elements and customization.

Scatterplots: geom_point()

  • Begin with the call to ggplot.
ggplot()
  • Inside, put the name of the dataset.
ggplot(penguins)

  • At this point, running the code returns a blank gray square.
  • Add the variables you want to include inside the aes argument after the dataset. We will start with flipper_len as the variable on the x-axis and body_mass as the variable on the y-axis.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass))

  • Now the names of our variables appear on the axes, and the numbers on the axes are ranges that will include all of the data for these variables, but we have not yet added our data.
  • To make our data actually appear on the plot, we have to add a geometric object, or geom.
  • For a scatterplot, this is geom_point.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()

  • It’s customary to create a new line after each + in a ggplot call. Right now it doesn’t matter much, but the more elements you add to your plot, the larger the chunk of code gets, and it becomes much easier to read when there is one element per line.
  • Right now, this plot doesn’t tell us much, except that penguins with longer flippers tend to weigh more.
  • We can see that our dataset includes data from three different penguin species. Let’s color code the graph by species.
  • To do that, we add another variable to our aes argument, this time called color.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point()

  • What can we tell from this plot?
  • Try switching out the variables to look at other relationships in the dataset. You can use bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, and body_mass as numeric variables, and species, island, sex, and year as categorical variables.
# your code here
  • Right now, the labels on the axes are using the default names for the variables, all in lowercase with underscores between the words. Let’s clean those up.
  • To apply labels, we can add another line with the labs element, and specify what we want the text to be for the x, y, and color variables.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", color = "Species")

  • You can also use xlab and ylab to specify the x and y-axis labels. Either way works perfectly well!
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Flipper length (mm)") +
  ylab("Body mass (g)") +
  labs(color = "Species")

  • Let’s add a title as well.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", color = "Species", title = "Penguin Size by Species")

  • One last thing we can do to make our graph look more aesthetically pleasing is the change the theme.
  • Right now, the default is theme_gray.
  • The other preset themes are theme_bw, theme_classic, theme_dark, theme_light, theme_linedraw, theme_minimal, and theme_void.
  • Pick your favorite! (My choice is usually theme_light.)
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", color = "Species", title = "Penguin Size by Species") +
  theme_light()

  • And there you have a completed graph!
  • Bonus: There are many small tweaks you can make to a graph to make it look even better, such as by changing the font size, adding extra white space around the axis labels, centering the title, etc.–these are mostly covered by setting parameters in the theme argument.

Bar graphs: geom_bar()

  • There are two different types of bar graphs you can make using geom_bar().
    • Frequency bar graph: counts how frequently each category within a variable occurs
    • Summary bar graph: gives a summary statistic for each category within a variable
  • geom_bar uses the argument stat to tell it how to calculate the height of the bars.

Frequency bar graphs: stat = "count"

  • This graph shows the frequencies of one or more categorical variables (below, species).
  • geom_bar has an argument called stat that you usually have to specify. For this type of bar graph, it is stat = "count".
    • "count" is the default, so you do not have to include it.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count")

  • To make each bar a different color, you can also assign the x variable to fill.
    • color is used to color points and lines; fill is used to color 2D shapes.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count")

  • Bonus: You don’t need the legend since the species are already listed on the x-axis; use the code below to get rid of it.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

  • You can also use fill to include an additional variable, as below. (In this case, you do need the legend.)
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count")

  • Notice that some of the penguins’ sex is unknown and marked as NA.
  • To exclude the NAs, you can use the dplyr function filter along with the is.na function. The ! means “not”, so !is.na means “is not equal to NA”.
penguins_noNA <- penguins |> filter(!is.na(sex))

ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count")

  • By default, geom_bar will stack colors on top of each other. To put them in side-by-side columns, use position = "dodge".
ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count", position = "dodge")

  • Add labels, a title, and a theme to make the graph look better.
  • In addition to a title, you also have the option to add a subtitle.
ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = species, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count", position = "dodge")  +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count", color = "Sex",
       title = "Penguin Sample Frequencies", subtitle = "geom_bar(stat = \"count\")") +
  theme_light()

  • Try switching out the categorical variable with island, sex, or year to look at other frequency distributions.
# your code here

Summary bar charts

  • The second kind of bar graph has two variables: a categorical variable and a numerical variable.
    • ex. height by species
  • There are two different stats that can be used to create this kind of bar graph: stat = "identity" and stat = "summary".
    • identity is used when you have only one data point for each category (ex. land area by continent)
    • summary is used when you have multiple data points and want to summarize them. You then have to specify how you are summarizing them (e.g. average, median, sum, etc.) using fun.

stat = "summary"

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = mean)

  • Again, we can add an additional variable using fill. (If using sex, return to the filtered dataset.)
  • Remember to use position = "dodge" to put the columns side by side. It doesn’t make sense to look at the total mass of male + female penguins in this context!
ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = species, y = body_mass, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = mean, position = "dodge")

  • Add labels and a theme.
ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = species, y = body_mass, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "summary", fun = mean, position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Body mass (g)", fill = "Sex",
       title = "Body Mass by Penguin Species", subtitle = "geom_bar(stat = \"summary\")") +
  theme_light()

  • Try switching out the variables to look at other relationships in the dataset. You can use bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, and body_mass as numeric variables, and species, island, sex, and year as categorical variables.
# your code here

stat = "identity"

  • Another way of generating this type of graph is by summarizing the dataset in advance, so that there is only one point per category, and using stat = "identity".
  • You do this by using the dplyr functions group_by and summarize.
penguins_summary <- penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(species) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len))

ggplot(penguins_summary, aes(x = species, y = flipper_len_avg)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge")

  • The new dataset penguins_summary only contains the variables species and flipper_len, so if you want to include another categorical variable, you have to include it in group_by.
penguins_summary2 <- penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(species, sex) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len))

ggplot(penguins_summary2, aes(x = species, y = flipper_len_avg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge")

  • Add labels and a theme.
ggplot(penguins_summary2, aes(x = species, y = flipper_len_avg, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", fill = "Sex",
       title = "Flipper Length by Penguin Species", subtitle = "geom_bar(stat = \"identity\")") +
  theme_light()

  • Note that if you want to switch out the variables using this method, you have to generate a new summary dataset.
  • stat = "identity can also be used in a case where there is only one observation per category e.g. land mass by continent
continents <- data.frame(continent = c("Asia", "Africa", "North America", "South America","Antarctica","Europe","Oceania"),
                         size = c(17226000, 11724000, 9360000, 6878000, 5500000, 3900000, 3286087))

ggplot(continents, aes(x = continent, y = size/1000000, fill = continent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  labs(x = "Continent", y = "Land Mass (million sq mi)", title = "Continental Land Mass") +
  theme_light() +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  • WARNING: If you use stat = "identity" when there is more than one observation, it will sum all of the observations together.
  • This can be useful if you need to calculate the total sum of a category, but none of the variables in penguins make sense to sum (we don’t need the total length of all the penguins’ flippers together).

Line graphs: geom_line()

  • Finally, the last main geom we’ll look at is geom_line.
  • Line graphs are typically used for data over time, so let’s jump to a new dataset, economics.
  • Find more information about this dataset with ?economics.
head(economics)
  • Plot unemployment by date.
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line()

  • Plot other variables (pce, pop, psavert, uempmed) by date.

  • The economics dataset doesn’t have any grouping variables, so to demonstrate how to add a third variable, we’ll return to penguins.

  • penguins only covers three years (2005-2007), so this will be a very simple line graph, and we’ll have to summarize to get an average for each year.

  • We can pipe |> that summarized dataset directly into ggplot without creating a new variable. Just leave the first argument out and start with aes.

penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg)) + 
  geom_line()

  • Add species as a grouping variable. Since we’re working with lines, use color.
penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year, species) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg, color = species)) + 
  geom_line()

  • Add labels and a theme.
penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year, species) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg, color = species)) + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", color = "Species",
       title = "Flipper Length by Penguin Species, 2005-2007") +
  theme_light()

Customization

  • You can customize the appearance of your graphs using additional arguments for color, shape, size, and more.
  • For purely aesthetic alterations (e.g. making all the points larger), you specify the arguments within the geom.
  • For variation that conveys information along an additional dimension, you specify the arguments in aes along with the variable you want it to depict, as we have already done using color and fill.

Aesthetics for geom_point

Manual customization of color

  • color can be specified by hex code (e.g. "#800080"), or by the name of one of R’s preset colors
  • List of colors: https://r-charts.com/colors/
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point(color = "cornflowerblue")

Manual customization of shape

  • shape can be specified by numeric code (see link below) or by word (e.g. “triangle”)
  • List of shapes: https://r-charts.com/ggplot2/shapes/
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point(shape = 17)

Manual customization of size

  • size is given as a number (default size = 1.5)
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)

Manual customization of transparency

  • alpha (transparency) is given as a number between 0 and 1
  • 0 = fully transparent, 1 = fully opaque
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3)

Variation by aesthetics

  • All of these aesthetics can also be used as axes of variation.
  • For categorical variables, color and shape work well.

color

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point()

shape

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, shape = species)) +
  geom_point()

  • Multiple aesthetics can be applied to the same variable to make the categorical differences even easier to see.
  • Useful when you want a graph to work in color and grayscale.
  • When this is done, the color and shape legends merge into one.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point()

  • For continuous variables, size, alpha, and sometimes color work well.

size

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, size = bill_len)) +
  geom_point()

alpha

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, alpha = bill_len)) +
  geom_point()

color

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = bill_len)) +
  geom_point()

Combination:

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, size = bill_len, alpha = bill_len, color = bill_len)) +
  geom_point()

  • You can use different aesthetics for different variables to get more than three axes of variation, but usually more than 4 will be hard for viewers to process.
ggplot(penguins_noNA, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass,
                          color = species, shape = sex, size = bill_len, alpha = bill_dep)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(legend.box = "horizontal")

Aesthetics for geom_line

Manual customization of color

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick2")

Manual customization of transparency

ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick2", alpha = 0.5)

Manual customization of line width

  • linewidth or lwd
  • given as a number (default size = 0)
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick2", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 2)

Manual customization of line type

  • linetype or lty
  • given as an integer from 0 to 6 or the name of the line type
    • 0 = “blank”, 1 = “solid”, 2 = “dashed”, 3 = “dotted”, 4 = “dotdash”, 5 = “longdash”, 6 = “twodash”
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick2", linetype = 2)

Variation by new aesthetics

  • Using linewidth as a dimension of variation:
penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year, species) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg, linewidth = species)) + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", color = "Species",
       title = "Flipper Length by Penguin Species, 2005-2007") +
  theme_light()

  • Using linetype as a dimension of variation:
penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year, species) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg, linetype = species)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", color = "Species",
       title = "Flipper Length by Penguin Species, 2005-2007") +
  theme_light()

  • Including both color and linetype:
penguins_noNA |>
  group_by(year, species, sex) |> 
  summarize(flipper_len_avg = mean(flipper_len)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = flipper_len_avg, color = species, linetype = sex)) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Flipper Length (mm)", color = "Species",
       title = "Flipper Length by Penguin Species, 2005-2007") +
  theme_light()

Aesthetics for geom_bar

Manual customization of color

  • Use fill for the inside of the bar.
  • Use color for the outline of the bar.
  • Both use the same set of color names.
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1") +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(color = "goldenrod1") +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1", color = "black") +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

Manual customization of line width

  • Affects the outline of the bar
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

Manual customization of transparency

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1", color = "black", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

Manual customization of width

  • width is given as a number from 0 to 1 (default 0.9)
    • Bars of width 1 will touch each other
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1", color = "black", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5, width = 1) +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "goldenrod1", color = "black", linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.7) +
  ggtitle("Penguin Sample") +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Count") +
  theme_light()

Exporting an image file

  • To look at your plot, click the Zoom button.
  • As you drag it around, notice that as you resize the window, the font becomes larger or smaller in relation to the graph. To get the proportions right, change the dimensions of the window.
  • One way to save your plot as a file on your computer is to right-click on the zoom window and choose “Save image as”. If you do it this way, make sure to type the extension you want into the name of the file (e.g. .jpg, .png)
  • Another way to save your plot is to click the Export button and choose “Save as image”. Here you can choose the file type and explicitly specify the dimensions you want for your image, in pixels.
